title: AI Detection Debates Are Really About Who Decides
summary:
rss · Sean Goedecke · Nov 27, 00:00

**「Background」** Disputes over whether a prize-winning story, manuscript, or tweet was written by AI keep recurring, often centering on detection tools such as Pangram. Sean Goedecke argues that arguments about reliability or ethics are downstream of a deeper conflict over who has the power to decide what counts as AI-written.

**「Solution」** He tries to steelman anti-AI skepticism: if AI threatens public discourse by concentrating social power in the tech sector, then making another tech company the arbiter is not reassuring. Distrust of "tool-shaped" solutions is also rational for people who believe decades of software-mediated processes have eroded human, community-based judgment. But Goedecke parts ways with AI critics because the only alternative to detection tooling is community self-policing, and he contends that people who do not use AI are poor at spotting it—mistaking fluent, polite text for AI or missing obvious tells. He therefore favors Pangram as the best current tool, while acknowledging debate over its reliability and arguing that those who distrust tech companies should push for open-source or government-built detection rather than abandon detection altogether.

**「Takeaway」** His conclusion is that rejecting AI detection does not escape the power question; it simply hands judgment to communities that may get it wrong. Legitimate detection, in his view, requires better and more publicly accountable tools, not less detection.
